In brief

After mention of the matter of "forbidding Irish games in the park," talk in the bar turns to a more general discussion of natively Irish sports. Joe Hynes praises the Citizen for having promoted the playing of these ancient games: "There's the man [...] that made the Gaelic sports revival." And indeed Michael Cusack, the man on whom the Citizen is modeled, did co-found an organization called the Gaelic Athletic Association to help de-Anglicize Ireland. It has proved phenomenally popular, though the range of sports played today may not perfectly reflect Cusack's vision.

At more length

Today the Gaelic Athletic Association has more than half a million members. Its clubs, stadiums, and playing grounds can be found in every county of the republic, and it is headquartered in Dublin's Croke Park, a stadium that seats more than 82,000 people. This great success story began in 1884, when Michael Cusack and six other men met to plan a patriotic organization that would wean Irish men and women from English sports like cricket, field hockey, and polo and get them playing homegrown sports like hurling, handball, and Gaelic football. After Hynes raises the topic, the narrator recounts how "they started about Irish sports and shoneen games the like of lawn tennis and about hurley and putting the stone and racy of the soil." "Shoneen" here is a contemptuous way of referring to English games and the would-be-English men and women who play them.

One shoneen game in particular, "lawn tennis"—a somewhat more genteel version of the fast and athletic modern game—stands in for all effete English sports in the narrator's mind, much as it served to mock the preciosity of Alfred, Lord Tennyson's verses in Stephen's. Few greater antitheses to lawn tennis can be imagined than "hurley," or hurling, an astonishingly fast and rugged Irish stick and ball game that dates back at least to the Middle Ages. Stone putting too is an ancient Celtic sport, still practiced today at Scottish Highland games. Instead of putting a standardized metal "shot" (the modern sport at which the Citizen has excelled), true stones of various sizes are thrown for distance. Most do not exceed about 30 pounds for men (18 for women), but some are truly gargantuan—enough so to recall the boulder that Polyphemus throws at Odysseus's ship.

"Racy of the soil" is not a sport but an adjectival description. The OED notes that "racy" people, plants, animals, and drinks are full of sap, tasty, vigorous, or superior, and that the phrase "Racy of the soil" was used in the late 19th century to mean "characteristic of a certain country or people (chiefly used with ref. to Ireland)." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that the phrase was "used by Archbishop Thomas Croke (1824-1902) in the letter he sent Michael Cusack in December 1884 accepting the invitation to become the first patron of the Gaelic Athletic Association. They quote from Croke's letter as reported in an essay by David Greene, "Michael Cusack and the Rise of the G.A.A.," in The Shaping of Modern Ireland, ed. Conor Cruise O'Brien (1960): "'field sports as lawn tennis, polo, croquet, cricket and the like—very excellent [...] in their way, still not racy of the soil, but rather alien, on the contrary to it, as are, indeed, for the most part, the men and women who first imported and still continue to patronize them' (79-80).

Dublin's Croke Park was named for Archbishop Croke in 1913, after the GAA purchased the land. The link between a sports stadium and a prince of the church memorializes the way in which the GAA and the Gaelic League looked to clergymen for approval in Joyce's day—a fact which he mocks in the parody that follows the talk of ancient Irish games.

John Hunt 2026
